blocks.text: MS BELINDA WILLIAMSON (recalled)
Examination-in-chief by MR ASTBURY
Could you state your name for the record, please?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Belinda Williamson.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: Thank you. Nurse Williamson, we have heard from you before. In fact we heard from you last week about a baby named [Baby L] and your involvement with [Baby L] on the day of 9 April 2016. You touched on your involvement with his twin
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: brother, [Baby M]. You have been invited back told to deal specifically with [Baby M] so I'm going to ask you some questions about that, please. And in so doing I might cover some of the ground we covered last time, but only as a refresher and, I hope, to assist you as well in your recollection.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You were working a day shift on 9 April 2016; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: I'm going to ask Mr Murphy, please, to go to tile 80 to begin with. We can see through the swipe data you arrived at the neonatal unit at 7.28 am that morning; is that consistent with your routine?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Probably, yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: Good. If we can go, more importantly, please, to tile 83 and if we can remind ourselves of who was on duty that particular day. We've been through the doctors. For your benefit we can see that the shift leader that particular day was [Nurse B].
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: [Baby M]'s designated nurse was Mary Griffith. Also on duty, as far as registered nurses, Lucy Letby, Belinda Simcock, yourself -- apologies, your name appears in your former name -and Ashleigh Hudson. And then we have, as a nursery nurse, Angela McShane.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Had you had -- sorry, yes, let's look at the allocations just to remind ourselves again. If we can look to the right in nursery 1, we can see both [Baby M] and [Baby L], as you confirmed last time, were under the care of Mary Griffith. There were two other babies in room 1 under the care of Lucy Letby. And if we go clockwise around the form we can see in nursery 2, your colleague [Nurse B], with --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We've looked at this several times now.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: We can just see where -- you were in nursery 3 and responsible for three babies.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Now, on the last occasion you showed us a plan, which I'm going to ask Mr Murphy to remind us of, please, at J18122. If we can zoom in, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: You pointed out to us on the last occasion that there should be a door where the letter E --
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: -- appears on your plan. But can I just confirm with you, as you told us last time, that baby A in the right-hand corner, was that one of the babies under the care of Lucy Letby?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: B and C, I think, are [Baby M] and [Baby L] respectively?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: Did you have any contact with [Baby M] during the course of the day shift up until around 4 o'clock?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Not that I remember.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: Did you have any dealings with the baby appearing here as A on the plan during the course of that day shift?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: Briefly, please, what was the contact with baby A as they appear on your plan?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I was trying to re-site a cannula.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: Had anyone drawn your attention to that issue?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. Lucy had asked me to come and have a look at the baby and review it and then the cannula had gone, so I was trying to get a new cannula in.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: Right. Was it just a cannula that was causing concern?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, it was just the general -- that and the appearance of the baby.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: And what was the appearance of the baby?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: From what I can remember, pale, mottled, just not quite right, oedematous.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: Was your attention drawn to [Baby M] at that stage or at any other stage before 4 o'clock?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: You told us last time that about 4 o'clock there was an event involving [Baby M].
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: Before we leave the plan, could you tell us what additional information appears on there in relation to that incident?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I was just stood at E, talking to Mary and Lucy.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: Where you've told us there was a doorway?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: It's missed off the plan.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: Where were Mary and Lucy, just remind us?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Just at the medication bench, so just inside the door on E.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: Standing together?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: And just so we can distinguish it in comparison, perhaps, to other accounts, where would the nursing desk be in relation to that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So at the doorway the nursing desk, as you go in, is to the right.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: If we look at D, is it on the other side of the wall from where you've drawn that D?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, it's...
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: There's a mouse there if that assists.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The nursing bench is here (indicating).
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: Sorry, I was asking about the desk.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The desk? It was here (indicating). They were here at the nursing bench doing medications, fluids. I was stood in the doorway and they were here (indicating).
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: Thank you. What did you first notice at 4 o'clock of concern reading [Baby M]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: There was an alarm alarming on the baby.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: What was that alarm in relation to? Could you tell at that point?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think, from memory, it was a bradycardic alarm so the baby had become bradycardic.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: Remind us what bradycardia is.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Low heart rate.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: Right. What, if anything, did you do when the alarm went off?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Nothing, because Lucy had responded to it, she walked across the room to answer it.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: We've heard, and I think it was accepted, that Mary Griffith at that point was in the process of preparing a dextrose bag --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: -- and as a consequence was in sterile clothing or protective sterile clothing?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: What did she do?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: She -- because the alarm wasn't correcting, she walked over behind and helped Lucy.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: Did you get involved with [Baby M] at all?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: What did you do, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: From reading my statement, it said that as they tried to get the Neopuff the mask had dislodged and landed somewhere, so I went and grabbed a spare mask as per Mary's request.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: Let's pause there. Tell us then first before I deal with what you did, what did Mary and Lucy do when they got to [Baby M]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I couldn't see exactly what they did, but I'd assume they'd do what we normally do, which is assess the baby, try and make them respond, so you give them a tickle, touch them, trying to get their heart rate back up.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: You mentioned a mask. Tell us about that, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So the mask attaches to the Neopuff, so it's a face mask. Quite often we loop them in through the back of the incubator so they're -- sometimes if -- they just fall off, as if you've moved them. They can dislodge.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: I'm imagining, correct me if I'm wrong, there's a tube --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: -- that comes from the source at the wall?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: And the mask is a consumable, I think we have heard is the term?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: So that's attached to the end of the tube to then be applied to the baby?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: So when you talk about the mask falling off, is that the consumable --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's the consumable that fits on the end, yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: So that's come loose for some reason?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: Did you see how that happened?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: So you assisted by, what --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Mary had apparently asked me to just grab another one in the correct size.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: All right. And are you able to remember how long that took?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It doesn't take long because they're usually in the room, there's spares in the room on the resus trolley if you need them.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: So a matter of walking to wherever they were in the room?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And just picking it up and handing it over.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: You assisted with the mask? Did you notice what they did once you had handed the new consumable over to them?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: What did you do then?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I went back outside. I think --I don't know, but I may have called the twos if they had asked for it, which is the emergency number. But I have gone back outside and I would have shouted for [Nurse B] to come back in if she wasn't in the room.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: Was [Baby M], when you were in the room, responding in the way that was hoped?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't remember.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: Presumably the situation was persisting if you were calling others and you may have called the twos.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: Anything you can tell us about how things progressed from there?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: Do you recall assisting with [Baby L] at that stage?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: What did you do?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I took over making the fluids up.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: Would you have remained at the workstation that you've pointed out at point D?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No. I came back out because I need to listen out for the other nurseries.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: Because obviously other babies (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Still yeah (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: -- require attention while others are drawn to --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The emergency.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: -- the emergency in room 1?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: So you went elsewhere. Did you pick up where Mary had left off or did you have to start again?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Depending where she was up to I probably would have started again because I wouldn't know here she was up to. So if she has drawn fluids up into a syringe I don't know she's drawn up, when or how much, so --
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: It all depends where she was up to?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. So she may have just gotten the sterile stock out.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: She may not have yet opened it or started. So if she hasn't started --
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: You can't remember?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: Did Dr Jayaram attend the emergency?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: According to my statement, yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: Do you have any recollection of that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: Did you take any part in the resuscitation that followed?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: Did you ask anybody else, can you recall, anyone else on duty to complete any other tasks?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I asked Ashleigh to go up and get the parents so I asked her to run up the back stairs and get the parents.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: The parents were still?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Up on ward 32.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: Thank you. Ward 32 being?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Post-natal ward.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: Thank you. Because we've heard that [Baby M]'s mum was still an inpatient --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: -- at that point.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Did you at any point ascertain how well the resuscitation was progressing?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I know from my statement that I've said I heard, at one point, Ravi talking to the parents and they were talking about discontinuing if they didn't get a response.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: Did it strike you that it had gone on for some time at that point?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: Anything else, Nurse Williamson, you can recall that may help us with regard to the collapse of [Baby M]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: Thank you. If you could wait there, please.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Cross-examination by MR MYERS
I'm going to ask if we can keep the map on the screens, Mr Murphy. Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Just some questions first about the map, please.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: The positions D and E, position E is where you recall you were at the time [Baby M] collapsed; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: Do you recall in fact position D is where roughly you thought Lucy Letby and Mary Griffith were standing?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, because that's where the bench is, it's just inside those doors.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: That's why you marked it D because that's where they were?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: You have been asked about the positions of [Baby M] and [Baby L]. [Baby M] you put down at B and [Baby L] as C, didn't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I think so.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: And you've said that, that's not disagreeing with what you've said.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Just with regard to the position of [Baby M], and I know you've been asked questions about this, you've described to us that when the Neopuff was used at the time of the collapse it fell on the floor.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: Just a little more detail on that: there's a housing, a wall-mounted unit that the Neopuff mask will fix into, isn't there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: The actual machine, yes, so that didn't collapse on the floor, that stayed wall-mounted.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: But what happens is the baby will have a mask that's used for that baby?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: And so when a baby is put in a position in the nursery, if there's a mask that's for that baby, it will be attached to the wall-mounted unit nearest to their position; is that right?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: I'm going to suggest the reason the mask came detached was that [Baby M] was rather more into the corner than you've drawn it, so it was rather awkward to try and pull it round. Do you recall that being the case or not?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, I just thought it dislodged as they tried to get it through the incubator doors, which frequently happens because it's a small space and you are trying to get a piece of equipment through the top end of the incubator.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: So it dislodging is not something that's unusual?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: But because it had fallen to the floor, it was necessary to get another one --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: -- so it was clean?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: And that's why you did that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: And then events proceeded form there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: Thank you very much for that.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: With regard to the events in the nursery that day you recall at one point assisting Nurse Letby with a cannula for baby A, don't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: Do you recall whether there were parents in or around the nursery at that point or do you have no recollection?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No recollection.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: Right. When [Baby M] collapsed, you were standing close to Mary Griffith and Lucy Letby, weren't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: And you've described to us that you took over the preparation of the dextrose infusion for [Baby L], didn't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: When you were asked about that last week -- sorry, on 16 February, you told us that you may have thrown out the bag that they had been preparing.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: And you've repeated that today that you may have done that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: Just so the jury can understand, there's a reason why you may have done that, isn't there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. Because I don't know whether they've taken fluid out to put fluid in or where they're up to in the procedure, so rather than risk confusing the matter, you just start again, you throw -- and start from scratch.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: It's your name and signature that appears on the infusion record, doesn't it --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: -- when it's actually mounted, so you need to make sure it's right, don't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: And so for that reason you may well have started afresh when the task was handed across to you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I have no more questions. Does my Lord have any questions?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Questions from THE JUDGE
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Can you recall making up that infusion bag?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I know I was stood outside in the corridor making it up at a trolley, so I did move myself. I remember making it up —
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: Can you remember -- carry on.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: -- but not where I started from.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: Did you do that on your own?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: No, Ashleigh Hudson would have assisted me.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: Because we have heard it's a two-person job.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It would either have been before or after. I have a feeling it was after I had sent her up the stairs to get the parents. So I may have had prepared the trolley but wouldn't have started until she'd got back down.
blocks.speaker: WILLIAMSON

blocks.text: Thank you. That's all.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I haven't checked the list.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Possibility.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: You may be required again. So as I have said to you more than once before: please don't talk to anyone about anything to do with this case. Thank you very much for coming today.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (The witness withdrew)
Witness statement of MS ASHLEIGH HUDSON (read)
We're going to read some evidence next, please.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: In my Lord's bundle it's at page 5. The numbers are in the bottom right on this occasion. It's a statement from Ashleigh Hudson, dated 14 February 2018. She says this:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I have been asked for my recollections of 9 April 2016 in relation to the collapse of [Baby M] which took place in the neonatal unit at the Countess of Chester Hospital. To assist with my recollections, I viewed the nurses' notes for [Baby M] on 9 April 2016 though I do not appear on the notes.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I worked a 7.30 am to 8 pm shift that day in the neonatal unit. I had been on duty the previous day so I was aware that [Baby M] and his brother were admitted to the unit but I'd had no involvement in their care. I was [her recollection] designated two to three babies to care for in nurseries 2 or 3."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: My Lord, we've seen the representation of that:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "During my shift on 9 April 2016 I did not have any interaction with [Baby M]. At approximately 4 pm, I was in either nursery 2 or 3 when I heard a shout for help from nursery 1. I recognised
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: the shout to be from Lucy Letby and she shouted something like, 'Can I have some help please?' It was clear that the need for help was urgent, but there was no panic in her voice, which is normal, and something we all try to do to avoid alarming parents and others who may be on the unit. I immediately ran to nursery 1 and when I got to the door, I could hear the alarms going off [and she put in brackets] (heart rate monitor and oxygen saturation monitor) from inside. From the door, I could see that
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Lucy and Mary were at [Baby M]'s incubator and were commencing resuscitation. I cannot remember who was doing what task but they were both there. I think that possibly Belinda was also present in the room.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Resuscitation is a task that requires two people: one to carry out the chest compressions and one to operate the Neopuff, which gets air into the baby.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Lucy told me to crash bleep Ravi, referring to consultant Dr Ravi Jayaram. I knew that [Baby M] was suffering a cardiac arrest and not a respiratory arrest. I can't remember how I knew, whether someone told me or I knew because they were carrying out CPR. I went straight to the nurses' station and dialled 2222, which is the switchboard, and when they answered I said something like, 'Put out a crash call to paediatric consultant, cardiac arrest on neonatal'. The operator then repeated it back to me for accuracy and I hung up.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Ravi immediately rang back asking for information. I told him [Baby M] had collapsed but I didn't know why. He asked me to get more information while he made his way to the unit, so I ran back to nursery 1 and asked them what had happened. Lucy replied something like, 'We don't know, he's just suddenly collapsed, no warning'.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I returned to the phone and told Ravi that we didn't know what had happened and that it had been a sudden event. I told him they had started CPR and were drawing up adrenaline. Ravi replied that he was on his way. I then returned to nursery 1 and told them that Ravi was on his way.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "At that point someone, I can't remember who, asked me to run upstairs and get the parents. I went upstairs and asked [Baby M]'s dad to come with me. I took him downstairs via the staff back stairwell. A midwife brought mum down in a wheelchair, arriving a couple of minutes later.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The resuscitation of [Baby M] was ongoing and I offered my help, but I was told I wasn't needed. Clearly, despite the emergency, we still have responsibility for other babies in the unit, so I stayed outside preparing drugs for another baby with Belinda.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Whilst the resuscitation continued in nursery 1, I could see that Mary and Lucy were present. There was also a number of doctors present, one of which was Ravi, but I can't remember who the others were. The parents were also in the nursery, but I didn't see who was speaking to who."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: That concludes her statement, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Witness statement of DR CASSANDRA BARRETT (read)
If we could go forward to page 2, please, in the bundle. I'll read the statement of Cassandra Barrett.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Her statement is dated 3 February 2020. She says as follows:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I have been asked for my recollections of a baby by the name of [Baby M] who was born at the Countess of Chester Hospital on 8 April 2016. In order to assist my recollections, I have accessed [Baby M]'s medical records, though it is apparent I do not feature in the records so anything I say is purely from memory.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I attended the birth of [Baby M] on the 8th. I remember this was a twin birth and that it was uneventful with no issues identified that I remember.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "On 9 April 2016, I was the neonatal senior house officer on call, working a short day, which is an 8.30 am to 4.40 pm shift. Primarily, I was working upstairs on the post-natal ward doing the baby checks. I was holding the neonatal crash bleep, which meant that I would attend any delivery, but as I had been working upstairs I hadn't been downstairs on the neonatal unit prior to the events described below.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I do remember that at around 4 pm I was sat at the computer at the nurses' station on the neonatal unit. The station is next to nursery 1 with just a wall separating the station from nursery 1. As I was sat there I heard a shout for help come from nursery 1. The shout came with a sense of urgency and I know it was from a member of staff, but I don't know which member of staff it actually was and I don't remember the actual words used. I made my way into the nursery where I saw a number of staff members already present and beginning CPR on [Baby M], who was in an incubator in the top right-hand corner of the nursery as you enter it.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I do not know how many other babies were in the nursery, but I do remember that [Baby M]'s brother was in an incubator next to him. The only member of staff I can say who was present was Dr
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Tony Ukoh, who was the registrar. Dr Ukoh must have been on the unit when the call went out, possibly on a ward round, as he got to nursery 1 slightly before or at the same time as I did.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "There were nurses present but I cannot remember who they were. I'm unable to name any of them, partly through a lack of memory but also due to the fact I may not have known their names in the first place. I have no memory of which nurses were on duty that day.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I could see that [Baby M] was pale and floppy with no respiratory effort and a low heart rate. I would describe him as looking very, very unwell. He was being Neopuffed to inflate the lungs and, because there was very little heart rate, they began CPR. During this procedure Dr Ukoh began to intubate [Baby M] and at some point I took over the task of giving chest compressions whilst the nurses drew up the medication.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Eventually, six doses of adrenaline were given and two doses of bicarbonate. The consultant was called quite early on so at some point Dr Ravi Jayaram arrived. I can't remember the details of [Baby M]'s condition and how serious it actually was, but I do recall that the collapse was so serious that there were concerns (possibly from me, but possibly from others as well, I can't remember) that [Baby M] might not survive it.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Eventually, [Baby M] stabilised and then recovered quickly. His heart rate increased and colour returned to him. I did not stay for long after this as my shift had ended some time earlier. I do not think I had any further involvement with [Baby M] after this event until I carried out his newborn baby checks before he was discharged home."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: That concludes that statement. May I recall next, please, Dr Ravi Jayaram.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR RAVI JAYARAM (recalled)
Examination-in-chief by MR ASTBURY
Could you state your name, please, for the record?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Ravi Jayaram.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Before we begin, doctor, on a couple of occasions I have been guilty of not slowing you down so please bear in mind (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I will do my best to try and slow down.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: You've been invited along today to deal with events on 9 April 2016, which was a Saturday. And we understand that you were the on-call consultant for the NNU at Chester.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: The incident involved a baby by the name of [Baby M].
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Not to that point, no.

blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: So it's distinct from a weekday where there's a consultant --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: -- through the day and then you have --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And then someone takes over at 4 o'clock.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So you had been on throughout the day?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I had.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Had anything been brought to your attention regarding [Baby M] through the day?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, not at all.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Do you recall receiving a crash call that afternoon?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: According to the notes, yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: You have seen our presentations before.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: I'm going to ask you to have a look, please, at tile 151 just to keep our chronology, which suggests that you were bleeped at 16.04 that afternoon. Is that consistent with your recollection?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It is, yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Having received that bleep, do you recall what you were told at that stage before you attended the NNU?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't remember what specific message, verbatim, I was told, but I was told that [Baby M] had suffered a cardiorespiratory arrest and resuscitation had been commenced and would I attend.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Right. That sort of information, does that affect how quickly you get to the scene?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, you get there ASAP. If it was a Saturday, I have to admit I don't recall whether I was on site or at home or whether I was actually in the hospital elsewhere. So when we're on call on weekends, we'd go in in the morning, do the ward rounds, and then be available for calls at short or long notice depending on the urgency.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Okay. When you did arrive, do you recall what you found?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. So when I arrived, [Baby M] was receiving cardiopulmonary resuscitation. I recall that Dr Ukoh, who was one of our locum registrars, was leading things and Nurse Letby was there and other people, although I don't recall who. Dr Ukoh handed over to me what had happened to that point. [Baby M] was receiving cardiopulmonary resuscitation, Dr Ukoh had intubated.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: I'm going to take you to your note in a moment. Just before we do that, do you recall anyone else being present when you arrived?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: There will have been other people. I don't recall who was there.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Did [Baby M]'s parents arrive at any point?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: [Baby M]'s parents were present. I don't know if they were there at the time I arrived, but I remember them being there and I also remember [Baby M]'s aunt being there as well because I remember having a conversation and she told me that she was a pharmacist. It's one of those things I just remembered.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Okay, it sticks in the memory. All right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I cut across you. You had started to tell us what, I think, Dr Ukoh then did. If you have a clear recollection, more than happy, but if you'd rather go through your notes --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I would rather do it from the notes for being more accurate.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: I wonder in that case could we go, please, to tile 210, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's dated 8 April. But I think everybody agrees, having seen the note before and after, that's just an error on your part in making the note.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I assume it was.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: But we all agree this was 9 April. Is that written at 17 --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Written at 17.40.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: All right. We've heard from other doctors, and it may be your practice, that when there's an incident like this, the priority is treating the patient and the notes (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Absolutely. The notes are -- it's important to do the notes as soon as is possible. But other things in terms of clinical care, communication with parents and staff, takes priority.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So if you wouldn't mind, could you take us through your note and what you recall as a consequence?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So I received the call at 16.04 and arrived at 16.15.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: [Baby M] was a twin born at 33 weeks. He'd been stable throughout the day. It was handed over that slight abdominal decision tension and some increased aspirates had been noted but he had been stable. Then he suddenly became apnoeic and bradycardic at 16.02. CPR was commenced. Dr Ukoh intubated him at 10 minutes. And by the time I arrived, he'd already had three doses of adrenaline given and --
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Pause there, please. The physical resuscitation that he was receiving, the CPR, what does that tell you?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That tells me that number 1, [Baby M] was not breathing for himself. And number 2, that his cardiac output was not
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: sufficient to pump blood around the body to supply the organs of his body. So in this situation, obviously if there is no heartbeat, it's fairly obvious that the heart isn't pumping, but if the heart rate is low, effectively it has the same effect. So the purpose of CPR in this situation is to oxygenate and ventilate the lungs, to get oxygen in and carbon dioxide out, and then to essentially simulate the heartbeat and make the heart actually pump blood around the body to try to activate the brain and the rest of the organs.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: CPR, you've noted, started immediately. And then you went on, I think, to intubation?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. Well, Dr Ukoh intubated him. Now, intubation is never an essential thing. An airway can be managed with a Tpiece and mask or a bag-valve-mask, but intubation in this situation is useful because it means the airway is more secure and it can free up hands to do other things.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Okay. Is that a measurement at the end of the line?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: After where it says adrenaline?
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: No, "Intubated by Dr Ukoh". I think that then says, "Reg at..." and I can't see what --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Sorry, "At 10 minutes". So 10 minutes into the -- post the arrest.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So before you arrived?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Eleven minutes after the bleep?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Then I think it says, "When I arrived" -- is that adrenaline times 3?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That means by the time I arrived, three doses of adrenaline had already been given (overspeaking) 1 in 10,000, which is the standard preparation that would be used in a resuscitation.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: We've heard that there's a resuscitation trolley --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: -- with premade cartridges, is that right --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: -- available in the event there's an emergency --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: -- and they are premade and immediately accessible?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, and we know the doses that we give based on the weight of a baby.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Next, please, is that sodium --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Sodium bicarbonate.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Yes, and that would have been 8.4% sodium bicarbonate.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Remind us again briefly why sodium bicarbonate is important?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: In this situation, the aim of CPR is obviously to try and maintain a circulation whilst we are trying to get to a situation where spontaneous unassisted circulation can take place. In a situation where initial resuscitation and adrenaline has not been effective, we have to think, why isn't it effective.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: In these situations, when there's been a period of poor oxygenation of the organs of the body, a situation develops called acidosis, usually a metabolic acidosis, and that happens because the cells of the body rely on anaerobic respiration, which is basically the way that they can continue to work without oxygen. A byproduct of anaerobic respiration is lactic acid and in a situation where there's a metabolic acidosis that can impair cardiac function. So in a situation where we get this far in and adrenaline hasn't worked, we have to think, well, is one of the reasons adrenaline isn't working at this stage because the baby is so acidotic that we actually need to try and get round that acidosis.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So sodium bicarbonate is an alkaline fluid and the idea is to try and neutralise the acid and bring the pH, the body's acid levels, acid/base levels, back into the normal range.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Could we pause there, please? I'm going to ask Mr Murphy just to go to tile 171, please. I'm going to ask you to look, with those points you have just made, Dr Jayaram, at the blood gas record. It was taken at 16.22, so within 8 minutes of your arrival and during this --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: During the resuscitation.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So it's the fifth entry down I'm sure you can see. It's dated and timed. It's a capillary sample, we understand?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: If you could talk us through those entries, please, in the context of what you just told us.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No problem. So if we look at the first column, the pH, which is 7.00. A normal bodies pH, if you do it as an arterial gas, would be between 7.35 and 7.45. Capillary gases are a different way of taking bloods. Often, the pH range is slightly lower than it would for an arterial blood, but a pH of 7.0 suggests a significant overall acidosis. So in this situation we can say that [Baby M] was acidotic.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: When we look at an acidosis, there are basically two systems in the body that can regulate the acid/base balance: the lungs, so we talk about the respiratory component, and the metabolic system, which is mainly your kidneys but there are other things in the blood as well that can affect the metabolic side of things.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: If we look at the pressure of carbon dioxide, that's 10.6 kilopascals. Normally a CO2 would be between 5 and 7. Sometimes in premature babies we do let the carbon dioxide run a little bit higher but that's a significant respiratory acidosis and that reflects that [Baby M]'s breathing wasn't as effective as it should have been.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: The PO2 of 3.34 is low, but on a capillary sample that's difficult to interpret because blood, as soon as it moves from the arteries to the capillaries, gives up its oxygen immediately, so we are relying more on looking at the oxygen saturation on the monitor.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: The sodium bicarbonate level is low and the base excess is minus 11.7. Base excess is a difficult concept to get your head around, but it is essentially a reflection of the metabolic component of the acid/base status. And again, it's usually between about minus 4/plus 4, there or thereabouts.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: It's looking for trends really. If we look at the gas at the top, say the 12.43 gas that's there from the 8th, that is a fairly normal capillary gas. If we look at the one at 16.22 we can see there's a significant metabolic acidosis. This is what one would expect to see during a period of cardiorespiratory arrest.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: This is at the time --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: This is during (overspeaking) yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: What does this tell you about [Baby M]'s health at that point?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Well, it tells us -- what we don't know is obviously what the gas was 2 minutes before that, 4 minutes before that, or at the time of arrest.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: It's a snapshot?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The snapshot tells us that he is very, very unwell.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: He's got a metabolic acidosis, which suggests that he has not been getting adequate delivery of blood and oxygen to his tissues and a CO2 of 10.66 is higher than it should be.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Now, one could argue is that because he wasn't being ventilated adequately? But if you are not getting blood perfusing to the lungs, you'll never have a normal CO2 during a resuscitation. The fact that his pH wasn't any lower than 7 in this situation is a good thing, but this is the blood gas of a very, very unwell child. And we'd call this a mixed acidosis.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: The other thing that's important is that we can see that the lactate, at the far right, was 9.8. So I mentioned that when cells are starved of oxygen, they rely on anaerobic respiration and a byproduct of anaerobic respiration is lactic acid and we can see that his lactate was high in this situation.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Okay. Thank you. So that's interpreted that for us.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Can we go back to your note, please, at 210.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: If we scroll down a little, Mr Murphy, please. We'd reached, I think, the sodium bicarbonate entry --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: -- leading us to the -- is sodium bicarbonate an alkali?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Sodium bicarbonate is an alkali? We gave that --
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Is that to adjust the pH --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. It will never be 100% effective because obviously there's ongoing anaerobic respiration. It's really just to try and bring the pH of the body up to try and improve the conditions to make the myocardium, the heart muscle, more able to beat spontaneously.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Thank you. Now, you've (inaudible: coughing) -- are these matters that were brought to your attention?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. These weren't noted by me, these are things that were told to me, that he'd had some bilious nasogastric aspirates and his abdomen had been distended throughout the afternoon.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: The next bullet point, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So I made the observation that he wasn't breathing spontaneously, which is why he was intubated and was having his breaths done for him. I commented that the heart rate was 60. Actually, what I recall is that although I have documented the heart rate was 60, my recollection -- and bear in mind this was a long time ago -- is on the monitor the electrical activity suggested a heart rate of 60, but actually there wasn't any detectable cardiac output apart from with CPR.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: That's a situation we call pulseless electrical activity. So the electrical conducting system of the heart is working and you can pick that up on the ECG, but it's not effective in actually making the myocardium, the heart muscle, contract effectively to pump blood around the body.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Electric pulses but no pumping as a result?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. And in some situations, even if the heart was pumping, the pumping of the heart was clearly inadequate so either way, the treatment and the interventions are the same.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Okay. After you've noted -- you note the heart rate at 60 --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: -- from the monitor that you've told us. What's the next entry, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So what I said is I documented what happened through the rest of the resuscitation, so CPR continued at intervals.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: [Baby M] received further adrenaline. He had another round of sodium bicarbonate as well. We also gave two boluses of normal saline. So normal saline is -- 0.9% saline is a fluid that essentially is isotonic, so it's the same concentration as the fluid that -- as blood, basically. The idea of giving fluid again in an arrest situation is that one of the things -- you have heard me talk before about Hs and Ts.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: One of the things that can potentially cause arrest is hypovolaemia, not enough fluid being in the circulation.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Again, we give a bolus of saline on the assumption that one of the things that could be a problem here is the fact that there's not enough fluid in the circulation, let's bolster up the circulation. So he received two 10ml per kilogram boluses in the period --
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: I'm going to interrupt you there, doctor. I'm sorry to do so. I'll come to the end of the resuscitation in a moment.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's the entry after you've recorded the heart rate of 60 that I was interested in. Tell us what that says, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Good air entry with IPPV."
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So IPPV means intermittent positive pressure ventilation, which is essentially what [Baby M] was receiving down the endotracheal tube. So he was basically having his breathing done. When I say there's good air entry, that means when I listen with a stethoscope I can clearly hear air going in and out of each lung. So again we know, whatever else may be going on in this situation, that there isn't an issue with the airway being blocked and there's not an issue, obviously, with the lungs because we can hear gas going in and out.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So air, thus oxygen, going in and out of the lungs --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: -- but as you told us before, the acidosis suggesting it's not finding its way to the tissues?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's two things really: we can hear gas going in and out of the lungs and I haven't said what, but I would assume we would have been resuscitating in oxygen rather than just air at this point.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So the fact that we know that gas is going in and out of the lungs but we are not -- we are still not getting great oxygenation -- we've still got quite a significant respiratory and metabolic acidosis -- would suggest that there is an issue
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: here with blood actually perfusing the lungs to pick up that oxygen.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Now, that can happen because if the heart is not beating then clearly we can put gas in and out of the lungs but there's no blood going through to give up carbon dioxide for the lungs to blow out and there is no blood going into the lungs to pick up the oxygen that we're putting in.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: The idea with CPR is you're trying not only to get blood around the body, but obviously you have trying to get blood from the heart to the lungs as well.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Okay. You were telling us about the various doses of adrenaline and saline that [Baby M] received during his resuscitation. Did the resuscitation go on for some time?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I think it was close to 30 minutes. And I recall this: that we were in a situation where, in spite of our interventions, we weren't really seeing any kind of response in terms of heart rate or spontaneous respirations. Generally, in this situation with resuscitation, one of the things we have to start considering is what is the likely outcome going to be of this resuscitation. And obviously what we want to do is get babies back round ASAP.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Generally, the longer a resuscitation goes on for, the less likely it is to have a good outcome, number 1, in terms of actually a spontaneous circulation returning, and number 2, in terms of subsequent neurodevelopmental outcome. And generally, in neonatology, we start thinking after about 20 minutes, what is the right thing to do here. And I recall discussing with [Baby M]'s family that at some point we might need to consider stopping resuscitation and thinking, are we actually going to turn things around.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: I remember discussing with the team that we might have to do that. Now, these decisions are very, very difficult and they have to be a collaborative decision, all decisions around care of babies have to be collaborative decisions. You know, it's not my job as the senior person there to dictate what needs to be done and families need to be part of this decision-making process. And of course this is difficult because these are decisions that have to be made with very much -- not very much time.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And we'd reached a point where I thought, actually, we're going to have to think about withdrawing. Then for no -- I mean thankfully, but not because we'd made any one specific further intervention, [Baby M] suddenly recovered and his heart rate
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: came up and he started breathing and we could actually stop CPR in the sense that his circulation became adequate again --
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: -- which I was glad about, but I wasn't sure what it was we'd done to suddenly make him better.

blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Right, okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And those are all potential consequences of having had a period of poor oxygenation of the body's organs.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So one can anticipate problems with the kidneys because you can get kidney failure as a result of poor circulation and poor oxygenation. blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: This is a discussion I had with [Baby M]'s parents after circulation was restored.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Right. The priority being to restore circulation?

blocks.text: Yes. Essentially, bring [Baby M] out of cardiorespiratory arrest or out of cardiac arrest.

blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: We talked about his abdominal problem because there had been this issue with him having had abdominal distension but certainly when I got there, unlike some other cases, his abdomen hadn't been hugely distended, and again, up to the point that arrest happened, and again bear in mind I wasn't there, there hadn't been any particular concern that his abdomen was so distended that it was impacting on breathing.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Right. If we complete your note, and I'll go back to the point you were making a few moments ago. Scroll down, please, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So the plan really was, obviously we'd restored circulation, which was a relief, beyond relief, and I was really pleased that we'd done that. It felt appropriate, even after the situation, we keep him ventilated because the important thing is to get the circulation back. It can take a bit more time for respiration to come back spontaneously. And it makes sense to maintain the airway and control the airway until we get an idea of which way things are going.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: I felt it would be appropriate to do an X-ray of his chest and abdomen to see if there were any obvious problems in terms of lung collapse, pneumothorax, bowel obstruction. blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: I said that, based on what I'd said to his parents, and we know that myocardial function can be impaired, that we needed to watch what his blood pressure and urine output were doing, and think about inotropes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Inotropes are medications that enhance the function of heart muscle and, if we needed them, then we could (inaudible) them. And again, keep an eye, have a low threshold or anticonvulsants. Anticonvulsants are drugs that we use if a baby is having seizures.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So really at this point, he was as good as we could be. And I would like to say at this point that I think that the team that actually resuscitated him did a very, very good job and the very fact that circulation was restored was a credit to what they did because it is unusual in a resuscitation that has had to go on for as long as this to get a return of circulation.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Okay. Again, I just to finish your note before we go back to the point we were discussing.

blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Distended bowel loops in this situation, given at the start of resuscitation [Baby M] was receiving breaths via a mask rather than the tube, we aim -- we do that to get gas in and out of the lungs, but obviously some of it is going to go down the oesophagus, the food pipe, into the stomach and into the intestine. blocks.text: I'm going to interrupt you. I think you were asked that question on the last occasion.

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. I can tell you the events around this as well because I was quite -- I'm trying to think of the appropriate word. I was quite confused in the initial testimony because I was being told that I absolutely knew the clinical significance

blocks.text: of this because I'd said in a statement we'd looked at these cases and found this.

blocks.text: And you've been reminded that you worked a night shift between 8 April of that year into the morning of 9 April that year?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: THOMAS

blocks.text: I'd like to ask you, please, whether at any time during the course of that shift you administered a baby by the name of [Baby L] with insulin.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, I didn't.
blocks.speaker: THOMAS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: No questions.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Thank you very much. That completes your evidence. I am told that you will not be required to give evidence again.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: THOMAS

blocks.text: If that changes, you will be notified, but I was told you would not be required again. But just in case -and it must be the remotest of possibilities -- you are required and out of an abundance of caution, don't talk to anyone about this case or anything to do with this case until it's finished, please. Thank you very much indeed.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (The witness withdrew)
Witness statement of MS SAMANTHA O'BRIEN (read)
My Lord, there are two statements we could read this afternoon.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Thank you very much, yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Beginning, please, with Samantha O'Brien, whose statement begins at my Lord's bundle, page 10.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: In a statement dated 31 October 2017, she says this:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I am making this statement in regard to my time working at the Countess of Chester Hospital where I was employed as a nurse in the neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I started full-time work at the Countess in January 2016. I worked there until July 2017. All of my time at Chester was spent working in the NNU.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I have been given copies of the nursing notes and would make the following comments.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby M]. I was not present for [Baby M]'s birth and did not care for him immediately. I came in for a night shift on 9 April 2016 and was assigned to be his designated nurse.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I was told that he had been very poorly during the preceding day shift and had been placed on a ventilator for my shift. He improved quickly during the night I cared for him and he came
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: off the ventilator at 3.30 am and on to CPAP. I don't know the specific details of the collapse during the day as I was not present for his resuscitation.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "His designated nurse who I took over from, who had been on duty when I collapsed, was Lucy Letby. I think another nurse had been caring for him in the morning, but Lucy took over when he became poorly as she had an extra qualification.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "It is normal for nurses to conduct a handover between shifts and I recall Lucy describing it as a 'long resuscitation' when we talked about [Baby M]. She told me that they had been just about to stop their efforts when they got a heart rate. I don't recall being told why [Baby M] had collapsed. To my knowledge it was never found out."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's the night shift of the 9th.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Witness statement of MS LAURA EAGLES (read)
If I could move to page 14, please, in my Lord's bundle. It is a statement from Laura Elizabeth Eagles dated 27 February 2018. She says this:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Further to my previous statement, I have been asked for my recollections of 10 April 2016 and, in particular, my recollections of a baby on the neonatal unit by the name of [Baby M].
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "To assist my memory, I have viewed [Baby M]'s nursing notes for that day. I am aware that [Baby M] suffered a collapse on 9 April 2016. I did not work on the 9th so I have no memory of [Baby M] prior to the 10th.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I would say that [Baby M] was in reasonably good health. He was still nil by mouth and he still had lines in providing medication and intravenous fluids. [Baby M] was still in nursery 1 and classed as intensive care.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I note from my nursing notes that I have made no specific entries in relation to the way he looked. This would suggest that his appearance was fine as I will always make entries noting any abnormalities or concerns.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I have been asked about the entry I made in the nursing notes at 17.38 in relation to apnoeas."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: My Lord, I wonder if we could pause there and just put up the relevant nursing note, please. It's at tile 401, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: In fact, it's timed at 17.28, my Lord. So the error is in the statement. But if we could look at the note, please, or certainly the first tile behind.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: If I can read it for the record:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Care taken over at 08.00. CBG at 08.00 not as good, so PEEP increased to 6.5 centimetres by [Dr A]. Repeat at 12.00 much improved. Has had 2 apnoeas, one needing vigorous stimulation and increased oxygen, and one needing Neopuffing. Commenced on caffeine by Dr Gibbs. Has been much better since. Resps remain between 20 to 30 per minute. Has been in air, 30% oxygen all day. Antibiotics given as prescribed. Cannula in right hand was puffy, so splint removed. Has flushed fine this afternoon. UVC in situ with TPN and lipid infusing. Limbs warm and pink. SBR remains below treatment line. Fluids increased to 90ml/kg, nil by mouth with minimal aspirates. Abdo non-distended. Passed urine. Bowels not opened."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Nurse Eagles continues:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I have viewed this entry and I can state there is nothing unusual about anything within the entry. All this is normal for premature babies and [does] not cause alarm. [Baby M] was started on caffeine at this time, which is the normal treatment for this. There were no significant events in relation to [Baby M] on the 10th and, given the fact that he had come off the ventilator quite quickly after suffering his collapse, I am of the opinion that [Baby M] recovered well from the collapse less than 25 hours earlier. I can also state that no concerns were raised by [Baby M]'s parents during visits."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: That concludes Nurse Eagles' statement, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: There's mention of Dr Gibbs in the note. We'll hear from Dr Gibbs tomorrow.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: But not available this afternoon?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Well, it's even shorter than I'd anticipated. Just in terms of tomorrow, obviously Dr Gibbs tomorrow. And are we then moving on to the experts?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes. Some more nurses to deal with, a discrete issue in respect of [Baby L], some more evidence read, and then we'll be moving on to Doctors Evans and Bohin.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: There we are. You know the pattern. So that'll be for tomorrow. All right? Thank you very much. Remember your obligations of which I reminded you briefly before the short break. 10.30 tomorrow morning then, please. Thank you very much indeed.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (In the absence of the jury)
I presume you would like to --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: There will be a brief visit, my Lord, yes.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Thank you very much.
